text: Java records make data modeling cleaner. But cleaner code does not automatically mean cheaper runtime behavior. One thing worth watching in record-heavy code is allocation rate. A record is still an object. It costs the same as an equivalent final class with the same fields. The issue isn't records. It's how many objects we create, and how often. If a hot path keeps creating new instances during mapping, filtering, aggregation, API transformations or event processing, the JVM ends up allocating a large number of short-lived objects. For example: Database Row ↓ Entity ↓ Record DTO ↓ Mapped Record ↓ Response Record Each transformation may create another object. Individually, that cost is small. The JVM is built for short-lived objects: allocation is a fast pointer bump, and a young GC mostly pays for the objects that survive. At high throughput, it still adds up: More short-lived objects ↓ Higher allocation rate ↓ More frequent young GCs ↓ Objects that live slightly too long get promoted to old gen This does not mean records are bad. It means immutability has a runtime cost when object creation becomes excessive. The JVM can remove some allocations through escape analysis and scalar replacement, but only when the code gets inlined and the object doesn't escape. Performance-sensitive code shouldn't assume every temporary object will disappear. For hot paths, I usually ask: 🔹 How many objects are created per request or event? 🔹 Are we repeatedly converting between nearly identical DTOs? 🔹 Are Streams creating intermediate objects or boxing primitives? (Stream<Integer> vs IntStream) 🔹 Is the allocation rate increasing GC frequency? 🔹 Can the same data flow use fewer transformations? Records are excellent for: ✅ Clear data contracts ✅ DTOs and API responses ✅ Events ✅ Immutable-style domain data But in a performance-sensitive path, the better question is not "Are records efficient?" It's "How many objects am I creating, and how often?" That's where profiling beats assumptions: JFR allocation profiling, async-profiler in alloc mode, or JMH with -prof gc. Clean code and efficient code are not opposites. But at scale, we need to understand the cost of the abstractions we choose. What's the biggest allocation surprise you've found while profiling?

text: Your safest parallel service calls might come from a try block, not a CompletableFuture chain. JEP 543, Structured Concurrency, is now proposed to become final in JDK 28, due in March 2027. After seven previews, from JDK 21 to JDK 27, no further changes are planned. That matters wherever one request fans out to several services. With ExecutorService and Future, if one call fails, the others keep running unless you cancel them yourself. The JEP calls this a thread leak. With StructuredTaskScope, you fork the calls inside a try block. If one fails, the scope cancels the rest, and no thread is left running when the block exits. The catch is that cancelled does not mean stopped. Cancellation is an interrupt, so a call that ignores interrupts keeps the scope open until it returns. A downstream service that already got the request may still complete it. I'd start with one endpoint that calls two or three services in parallel. I'd make one service fail and another hang, then check leftover threads, time to cancel, duplicate downstream work and the JSON thread dump. Only then would I set a scope timeout from the caller's deadline and delete the hand-written cancel code. A deadline only holds when every call under it responds to interrupts. Teams on JDK 25 can try it today as a preview, with small API differences. LTS-only teams will get it as final in JDK 29, due in September 2027. When one parallel service call fails, what cancels the others in your code today?

text: Cleaning a RAG corpus by deleting what looks bad is how you lose answers. Record a decision for every block instead, and leave the document intact. Most published cleaning recipes were built for training models on web crawls, where discarding a page is free because billions remain. A knowledge base has one copy of each answer. Four rules worth keeping: • Count the documents a block appears in, not its occurrences. A footer in all 19 articles is boilerplate. A safety paragraph repeated three times in one manual is not. • Never normalise digits away before hashing. "10 working days" and "14 working days" become one block, and the index keeps whichever it saw first. • A near-duplicate score measures shared wording, not agreement. Two paragraphs differing in one number can score about 0.95 and contradict each other, so compare the numbers first. • Presidio's default entity list includes dates and person names, which are often the answer. Pass an explicit list instead. text: Java 27 has no flashy new syntax. But it changes things that affect every Java app: memory, GC, and security. Here are 3 changes worth knowing: 1️⃣ Lighter objects by default (JEP 534) Every object in Java has a hidden header. Java 27 makes it 32 bits smaller (96 → 64). Multiply that by millions of objects, and your heap gets leaner. 2️⃣ G1 is now the default GC everywhere (JEP 523) The garbage collector cleans up unused objects in memory. Before, G1 was the default only in “server” setups. Now it’s the default in every environment. If you never set a GC explicitly, you now get G1 automatically. 3️⃣ Quantum-ready encryption (JEP 527) Attackers can save your encrypted traffic today and crack it years later with quantum computers. Java 27 adds a hybrid post-quantum key exchange to TLS 1.3, so today’s data stays safe tomorrow. text: A RAG change that fixes six answers and breaks three shows up as "+3". The three that broke ship unseen. RAG gets tuned one stage at a time: chunk size, embedding model, reranker. Every one of those changes moves every question at once, so judging it by a total, or by a few remembered questions, hides exactly the answers it broke. What I'd put in place before tuning anything: • A deliberately plain baseline: 400-token chunks, exact cosine search, top 5, no reranker. With no index, a missed passage is the embedding's fault, never the index's. • A golden set of 50-100 hand-written questions, each with its answer and the exact wording in the source that proves it • Match evidence on that quoted span, not a chunk ID. Every chunk ID changes the first time you re-chunk, which is exactly the change you're trying to measure. • Write the question before looking at the passage. Otherwise it reuses the passage's words, and retrieval looks better than real users will find it. The parts most eval setups miss: • About 1 in 5 questions should be unanswerable, on topic, with a plausible wrong answer nearby. Without them, missing content looks exactly like a working system. • Score correct, incorrect and abstained separately, and run once with retrieval off to catch answers coming from the model's memory • Run the unchanged baseline twice first. A change that flips fewer questions than a plain rerun has shown nothing. How do you know a RAG change actually helped, beyond the total going up? text: 🚀 Spring Boot & Hibernate: Understanding the N+1 Problem in Simple Words Have you ever wondered why your Spring Boot API is slow even when your SQL query looks simple? One possible reason is the N+1 Query Problem in Hibernate. Let’s understand it with a real-world example. 👇 👨‍💻 1. Imagine You Have 500 Employees Suppose your application has two database tables: 📌 Employee table Employee ID Employee Name Department ID 📌 Department table Department ID Department Name Now, you want to display all employees along with their department names. Sounds simple, right? But Hibernate might execute 501 SQL queries to get this information! 🤔 2. Why Does This Happen? First, Hibernate fetches all 500 employees using one query: SELECT * FROM employee; Then, when your code accesses each employee's department, Hibernate may execute another query to fetch that department. SELECT * FROM department WHERE id = 1; SELECT * FROM department WHERE id = 2; SELECT * FROM department WHERE id = 3; This continues for the departments that haven't already been loaded. So, in the worst-case example: ✅ 1 query to fetch employees ❌ 500 additional queries to fetch departments Total = 501 database queries! This is called the N+1 Problem. Here, N represents the number of employees, and 1 represents the initial query. ⚠️ If multiple employees belong to the same department, Hibernate may execute fewer additional queries. 💡 3. How Can We Identify This Problem? Sometimes, the API returns the correct data, but it takes too long to respond. Here are a few warning signs: 🔹 Your application executes hundreds of SQL queries for one API request. 🔹 Similar SQL queries run repeatedly with different IDs. 🔹 The API becomes slower as the number of records increases. 🔹 Your database receives more requests than expected. You can enable Hibernate SQL logging in your local development environment: spring.jpa.show-sql=true logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG This helps you see which SQL queries Hibernate is executing. 🛠️ 4. How Can We Fix the N+1 Problem? One common solution is JOIN FETCH. Instead of fetching employees first and then fetching their departments separately, we ask Hibernate to fetch both together. Example: @Query(""" SELECT e FROM Employee e JOIN FETCH e.department """) List<Employee> findAllWithDepartment(); Now, Hibernate can fetch employees and their departments in a single SQL query. Instead of making hundreds of database calls, we reduce unnecessary database round trips. Another option is @EntityGraph, which lets us specify which relationships should be fetched for a particular query. Batch fetching is also useful when we want Hibernate to load related data in groups instead of one at a time. ✅ The best solution depends on the data we need and how our application uses it. 📈 5. What Are the Benefits? ✅ Reduce unnecessary database queries ✅ Improve API response time ✅ Handle increasing data volumes more efficiently

text: Your next JVM startup win might come from a training run, not a native image rewrite. JEP 544, Ahead-of-Time Code Compilation, is now targeted to JDK 28, due in March 2027. text: Five ways to put a cache between your application and your database, and each one changes what you're trading away. Read-through: the application only ever talks to the cache, and the cache itself loads from the database the moment there's a miss. Cache-aside: the application owns that loading logic instead, checking the cache first and reading from the database itself on a miss, this is the one most teams reach for by default. Write-through: every write goes to the cache first, then immediately through to the database, so the two can never quietly disagree. Write-around: writes go straight to the database, skipping the cache completely, and the cache only gets populated later when that data is actually read. Write-back: writes land in the cache instantly and get flushed to the database asynchronously, which makes writes very fast and makes data loss possible if the cache fails before that flush happens. None of these is the "correct" one. Each is a different answer to how stale you can tolerate your cache being, and how much data you can afford to lose if something crashes at the wrong moment. Which of these five is your default, and which one have you actually been burned by?

text: Stop Choosing Databases Based on Trends. Choose by Architecture. In my 15 years as a Java Full-Stack Architect, I’ve seen teams tank their application performance before writing a single line of code. How? By picking a database because it’s "hyped" rather than analyzing their data access patterns. With the maturity of NewSQL, the decision isn't just a coin toss between SQL and NoSQL anymore. If you are architecting a modern system, here is how you should think about it: 1. Traditional SQL (Relational) =============================== • The DNA: Strict schema, ACID compliance, heavy relational integrity. • When I use it: Core transactional engines, ledger systems, ERPs, and complex cross-table joins. If absolute consistency is a hard requirement, SQL is the baseline. • Examples: PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle DB, MS SQL Server. • Java Stack Alignment: Spring Boot + Spring Data JPA/Hibernate + PostgreSQL. • The Trap: Vertical scaling limits. Sharding at scale becomes an operational nightmare. 2. NoSQL (Non-Relational) ========================= • The DNA: Schema-less, horizontally scalable, built for BASE (eventual consistency) and rapid high-volume writes. • When I use it: Large scale content catalogs, time-series telemetry, user sessions, and real-time caching. • Examples: • Document: MongoDB, Couchbase • Key-Value: Redis, Amazon DynamoDB • Wide-Column: Apache Cassandra, ScyllaDB • Graph: Neo4j • Search Engine: Elasticsearch, OpenSearch • Java Stack Alignment: Spring Data MongoDB / Cassandra / Redis. • The Trap: Simulating complex joins in your Java application layer because your document model wasn't designed around your read patterns. 3. NewSQL (Distributed SQL) =========================== • The DNA: The distributed horizontal scalability of NoSQL combined with the absolute ACID guarantees of traditional SQL. • When I use it: Global, distributed applications that require strict relational consistency but have traffic volumes that would break a traditional single-instance DB (e.g., globally distributed financial systems). • Examples: CockroachDB, Google Cloud Spanner, YugabyteDB, TiDB. • Java Stack Alignment: Fully compatible with standard JDBC drivers and Hibernate, making migration highly accessible for enterprise Java applications. • The Trap: Higher operational complexity and slightly higher write latencies due to distributed consensus protocols (like Raft or Paxos). The Architect’s Bottom Line: =========================== In modern system design, the answer is rarely a single database. We live in the era of Polyglot Persistence. I frequently design systems where a relational core handles user accounts and payments, Redis manages active sessions, and MongoDB or Elasticsearch powers the catalog and search. Don't fit your data into a trendy engine. Let your data's shape, consistency requirements, and growth map dictate the architecture.

text: Most RAG tutorials start with chunking and embedding. That's step two. Step one is deciding whether that work should happen at all, and when. Every RAG system parses, chunks and embeds at one of three moments: ahead of time for every document, per request for the few a question needs, or never, when documents go to the model whole. Most systems end up with one of these by default, not by decision. I wrote up a framework for choosing on purpose: - Profile each source first: size in tokens (not documents), change rate vs read rate, scope signal, latency budget, existing search, access control - Run four tests in order and stop at the first that passes: send everything → filter first → search the existing system → index everything - A later strategy isn't better, only heavier. Each one adds something to build, run and keep fresh. text: Your smallest Java pods may switch garbage collectors on the next JDK upgrade, without anyone changing a flag. Java 27, released in mid-September, makes G1 the default collector in all environments (JEP 523). Before this, the JVM picked Serial GC when it saw a single CPU or less than about 1.8 GB of memory. That matters more than it sounds. A Kubernetes pod with a CPU limit of 1 core looks like a single-CPU machine to the JVM. Many small services, sidecars and batch jobs have quietly run on Serial for years. The catch is that G1 everywhere does not mean every small service gets faster. G1 has improved a lot, but the JEP itself says some applications in constrained environments may still perform best with Serial. I'd start by checking which collector each service actually uses today. Running with -Xlog:gc at startup shows it. Then I'd compare Serial and G1 on one small service under the same load: p99 latency, container memory, CPU throttling and startup time. Only then would I decide per service. If Serial still wins, set it explicitly with -XX:+UseSerialGC. An explicit choice always overrides the JVM's default. Teams on Java 21 or 25 can run the same check now. It is the cheapest way to avoid a surprise when you move to the next LTS. Do you know which garbage collector your 1-CPU pods are running right now?

text: Most engineers leave load balancers on round robin and never touch the setting again. That default is quietly overloading your biggest server and underusing your smallest one, and almost nobody notices because the traffic "looks" evenly split. Round robin assigns requests sequentially, one to each server in strict order, regardless of what each server can actually handle or how busy it currently is. That's fine when every server is identical and every request costs the same. It falls apart the moment either assumption breaks. Weighted round robin fixes the capacity problem, distributing requests based on predefined server weights so a bigger box gets proportionally more traffic. But it's still static. It doesn't know that Server 2 is drowning in slow requests right now while Server 3 sits nearly idle. That's what least connections and least response time actually solve, and they solve different problems than people assume. Least connections routes to whichever server has the fewest active connections in real time, catching the case where one server is quietly backed up even though it received the same request count as everyone else. Least response time goes further, factoring in both current latency and connection count, so it can route around a server that's technically available but measurably slower right now. Neither of these is "smarter round robin." They're solving for real-time load, not request count. The other two algorithms aren't about performance at all, and conflating them with the first four is where teams get really confused. Source IP hash exists purely for session persistence, routing the same user to the same server every time so session state doesn't break. URL or URI hash routes based on the actual request path, sending /api traffic to one server pool and /images traffic to another, content-aware routing, not load distribution. The uncomfortable truth: picking an algorithm because it's the default, not because it matches your traffic pattern, is how "load balanced" systems end up with one server running hot while three others coast. Which algorithm is your load balancer actually running, and did anyone choose it deliberately? text: A REST API isn’t good just because it returns "200 OK". After working on backend systems for a few years, I’ve realized that writing the controller is usually the easy part. The harder part is designing an API that behaves predictably when things go wrong. For example, imagine a payment API: "POST /payments" The request reaches the backend, the payment is processed successfully, but the response times out before reaching the client. The client retries. Now the important question isn't whether the API returns "200". Will we process the payment twice? That’s where API design starts becoming interesting. 1. Validation should include business rules "@NotNull" and "@Size" are only the first layer. A request can be syntactically valid but still violate business rules — insufficient balance, invalid account state, transaction limit exceeded, or an operation that isn't allowed for that customer. 2. HTTP status and business status are different things Returning: "200 OK" "{ "status": "FAILED" }" for every scenario makes integrations harder to reason about. HTTP status should describe what happened at the protocol/API level, while the response should carry the relevant business outcome and error code. 3. Error responses should be contracts too Instead of returning different error structures from different endpoints, define something predictable: "errorCode" "message" "details" "correlationId" "timestamp" That correlation ID becomes especially useful when tracing a request across multiple microservices. 4. Idempotency matters once retries enter the picture Timeouts and network failures are normal in distributed systems. For sensitive operations such as payments or transfers, an idempotency key or unique transaction reference can help ensure: same request + same key ≠ duplicate transaction 5. Think about backward compatibility before changing DTOs Once another service or frontend consumes your API, the request/response contract is no longer just your implementation detail. Renaming a field, changing its datatype, or changing nullability can break consumers you don't control. 6. Design for operability, not just functionality A production-ready API should make it possible to answer: Which request failed? Where did it fail? Can it safely be retried? Structured logs, correlation IDs, metrics and meaningful error codes are part of API design too. That’s probably the biggest shift in how I look at APIs now: A working API handles the happy path. A well-designed API also defines what happens during retries, failures, invalid states and future changes. What’s one API design decision you started caring about only after working on production systems?

text: 🚀 Virtual Threads in Java 21 — What problem do they actually solve? Java 21 introduced one of the biggest improvements to Java's concurrency model: 👉 Virtual Threads 💡 What problem are Virtual Threads actually solving? Let's break it down. 🧵 First, what happens with traditional threads? Consider a typical backend request: Client Request ↓ Controller ↓ Service ↓ Database Query ↓ External API ↓ Response A request might spend only a small amount of time actually using the CPU. A significant portion of its lifetime could be spent waiting for: Database responses HTTP responses Network I/O File I/O Other downstream services During that waiting period, the platform thread assigned to the request is also effectively waiting. Now imagine your application receiving 10,000 concurrent requests. You can't simply keep creating more and more platform threads indefinitely. Platform threads are backed by operating-system threads and therefore have meaningful memory and scheduling costs. This is where things become interesting. 🚀 Enter Virtual Threads Virtual Threads are lightweight threads implemented by the JVM. They are not permanently tied 1:1 to an operating-system thread. Instead, the JVM schedules virtual threads onto a much smaller number of underlying carrier threads. Conceptually: Platform Threads Request 1 ──→ Thread 1 ──→ WAITING Request 2 ──→ Thread 2 ──→ WAITING Request 3 ──→ Thread 3 ──→ WAITING Request 4 ──→ Thread 4 ──→ WAITING ... ... More concurrent requests ↓ More platform-thread resources With Virtual Threads: Virtual Threads Request 1 ──→ Virtual Thread ─┐ Request 2 ──→ Virtual Thread ─┤ Request 3 ──→ Virtual Thread ─┼──→ Carrier Threads Request 4 ──→ Virtual Thread ─┤ Request 5 ──→ Virtual Thread ─┘ ... Thousands of lightweight tasks When a virtual thread performs a blocking I/O operation, the JVM can suspend it and use the underlying carrier thread for other work. That is the key idea. 🎯 So what problem does this solve? The primary goal is: ➡️ Handle a very large number of concurrent I/O-bound tasks efficiently. For example, imagine a microservice that receives requests and calls three downstream services: Request ↓ Service A ↓ Database ↓ Service B ↓ Service C ↓ Response If most of the time is spent waiting on these external systems, Virtual Threads can allow the application to handle many more concurrent operations without requiring a huge number of platform threads. And perhaps the biggest benefit is that we don't necessarily have to completely change the programming model.

text: 🚨 I had an API taking almost 4 seconds to respond. The strange part? CPU was sitting around 40%. So why was the API slow? 🔍 The first clue The service wasn’t busy computing. It was waiting. That changed how we approached the investigation. Instead of looking at algorithms, we started looking at what the request was waiting for. What the endpoint was doing The code looked completely normal: → Fetch a list of entities → Loop over them → Build DTOs Nothing suspicious at first. Until we looked inside the loop. ⚠️ Two expensive things were happening For every item: → A lazy relation was being accessed → another DB query → A synchronous HTTP call was made to another service And the external call was averaging around 350ms. With 15 items: 15 × 350ms = 5.25 seconds That’s potentially more than 5 seconds of sequential network waiting. But the network call wasn’t the biggest problem. 💥 The real problem The request was running inside an open transaction. Which meant it was holding a database connection while waiting for the network. The database wasn’t doing anything. The application wasn’t doing much either. But the connection was still occupied. Then concurrency made it worse Imagine a connection pool with 10 connections. 10 concurrent requests arrive. → 10 connections occupied → Each request waits on network I/O → The pool is exhausted → New requests start waiting → The queue grows → Eventually, requests time out The service looks overloaded. But it isn’t actually CPU-bound. It’s blocked. 💡 This is why metrics matter High CPU + high latency? The application may be doing too much work. Low CPU + high latency? The application may be waiting. That distinction can completely change where you investigate. The fixes We didn’t need a clever algorithm. We needed to remove the unnecessary waiting: → Fetch relations explicitly with JOIN FETCH or an EntityGraph → Batch external calls instead of making them inside the loop → Move network I/O outside the transaction boundary → Centralize exception handling so failures remain consistent → Cache read-heavy paths when a little staleness is acceptable 🎯 The lesson Never hold a database connection while waiting on the network. This kind of bug is dangerous because the code can look perfectly reasonable during review. Tests pass. Everything works with three seeded records. Then production brings: More data. More concurrency. More network latency. And suddenly… the same code behaves completely differently. Sometimes an application is slow precisely because… it’s doing nothing. I wrote the full walkthrough covering: → N+1 queries → Connection pool starvation → Transaction boundaries → Synchronous HTTP calls → The fixes with code Link in the first comment. text: You think your Kafka publish is safe inside @Transactional. It's not. @Transactional public Order placeOrder(...) { orderRepository.save(order); // ① DB write kafkaTemplate.send("order.placed"); // ② Kafka send } Two failure modes that WILL hit you in production: 💥 DB commits → JVM crashes → Kafka never gets the event 💥 Kafka send fails → Order saved → Event silently lost The Transactional Outbox Pattern solves this permanently. Write to DB + outbox table atomically. Let a scheduler relay to Kafka independently. Crash between the two? Scheduler retries on restart. Never lose a Kafka message again.

text: Your Stream didn’t promise the order you just observed. One of the easiest mistakes to make with Java Streams is confusing what happened with what the API guarantees. A HashMap may appear to iterate in the same order every time. A parallelStream() may print elements in order. findAny() may even keep returning the same element. None of these observations necessarily mean that order is guaranteed. In Part 2 of Java Internals, we go one level deeper: Where does encounter order actually come from? What does unordered() really do? Why can findAny() give the implementation more freedom than findFirst()? And why can a guarantee become a performance constraint? The mental model is simple: Guarantee → Constraint → Execution Freedom → Cost Senior engineers know what an operation does. Staff engineers also ask what constraints that operation puts on the execution.
